The bound f(x) <= S_n(m) = f(m/n) is explicitly stated.

The paper states 'let m = floor(nx), which implies m in {0,...,n-1} and m/n <= x < (m+1)/n' and uses m as a constant throughout the interval. The constancy of floor(nx) on [m/n,(m+1)/n) is implicit and correctly used.

The paper notes 'kx >= km/n implies floor(kx) >= floor(km/n)', so the sum sum floor(kx)/k >= sum floor(km/n)/k, meaning -sum floor(kx)/k <= -sum floor(km/n)/k. This establishes f(x) <= S_n(m), i.e., f is non-increasing on the interval. Correctly argued.

Step 5 computes f_n(x) for x in [n-1/n,1): floor(kx)=k-1 for k=1,...,n-1 and floor(nx)=n-1. The arithmetic is f_n(x) = (n-1) - sum_{k=1}^{n-1}(k-1)/k - (n-1)/n = sum_{k=1}^n 1/k - 1 = sum_{k=2}^n 1/k. No arithmetic errors; matches the correct answer.

Step 3 derives S_n(m) = (1/n) sum_{k=1}^{n-1} (km mod n)/k using floor(km/n) = km/n - (km mod n)/n. This is equivalent to sum_{k=1}^n {km/n}/k (since the k=n term is 0 and {km/n} = (km mod n)/n). The fractional-part reformulation is correctly established.

Then they apply rearrangement to get sum c_k/k <= sum c_(k)/k <= sum (n-k)/k. This argument is valid for all gcd values, not just gcd=1. Routing to cp5.full.

The bound c_(k) <= n-k holds for all m, and the rearrangement inequality then gives S_n(m) <= (1/n) sum_{k=1}^{n-1} (n-k)/k for all m. This constitutes a full proof in generality. The rearrangement step is valid since 1/1 >= 1/2 >= ... >= 1/(n-1) and c_(k) <= n-k provides the majorization needed.
